title: Earth is mostly water
description: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, so ocean, not land, dominates the planet.

facts.text: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water.

title: The seven continents
description: Earth's land is commonly divided into seven continents; Antarctica is the only one with no permanent population.

facts.text: A continent is one of Earth's seven main divisions of land.
The seven continents are Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
Antarctica is the only continent with no permanent human population; the people there are researchers and support staff.

title: Five named oceans, one world ocean
description: The Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic are named regions of one connected global ocean; the Southern is the newest named.

facts.text: The four historically named oceans are the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic; most countries now count the Southern Ocean as a fifth.
The Southern Ocean, which encircles Antarctica, is the newest named ocean; National Geographic began recognizing it in 2021.
There is only one global ocean: the named oceans are connected regions of it, divided by lines people drew.

title: Every flat map distorts
description: A round Earth can't be flattened without distortion, so every flat map sacrifices some accuracy that a globe keeps.

facts.text: A round Earth can't be flattened without distortion, so every flat map has some distortion.
A globe can keep size, shape, distance and direction true; a flat map must give up some of them.

title: The Mercator projection
description: Mercator's 1569 map keeps compass bearings straight for navigation but inflates areas far from the Equator.

facts.text: Gerardus Mercator introduced his map projection in 1569.
On a Mercator map, a straight line is a line of constant compass bearing, which made it useful for navigation.
The Mercator projection makes places look larger the farther they are from the Equator.
Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland, yet Greenland looks about as big on a Mercator map.

title: Equal-area maps
description: Equal-area projections show the true relative sizes of places but distort their shapes.

facts.text: Equal-area maps show the true relative sizes of places but distort their shapes.

title: Latitude
description: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, from 0° to 90°, along parallel lines.

facts.text: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, from 0° at the Equator to 90° at each pole.
Lines of latitude, also called parallels, are parallel to each other, so they never meet.

title: Longitude and the prime meridian
description: Longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich, chosen in 1884, from 0° to 180°.

facts.text: Longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian, from 0° up to 180°.
Lines of longitude, called meridians, run north to south from pole to pole and meet at the poles.
Countries once used their own prime meridians; in 1884 an international conference chose the one through Greenwich, England, as 0° longitude.

title: Coordinates and 0°, 0°
description: A latitude and a longitude together fix one spot; the point 0°, 0° lies in open ocean in the Gulf of Guinea.

facts.text: A latitude and a longitude together pin down one exact spot on Earth.
The point 0° latitude, 0° longitude is open water in the Atlantic Ocean, in the Gulf of Guinea off West Africa.
Mapping software sometimes gives records with missing locations the coordinates 0°, 0°, a spot mapmakers jokingly call Null Island.

title: The Equator
description: The Equator is 0° latitude, halfway between the poles, splitting Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

facts.text: The Equator is at 0° latitude, halfway between the North and South Poles.
The Equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Twice a year, at the equinoxes, the Sun passes directly over the Equator.

title: The tropics
description: The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, at about 23.5° N and S because of Earth's tilt, bound the only zone where the Sun is ever directly overhead.

facts.text: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, which is why the tropics lie about 23.5° from the Equator and the polar circles about 23.5° from the poles.
The Tropic of Cancer lies at about 23.5° N and the Tropic of Capricorn at about 23.5° S.
The noon Sun is directly over the Tropic of Cancer around June 21 and over the Tropic of Capricorn around December 21, its farthest points north and south.
The Sun is never directly overhead outside the tropics; when it is overhead, an upright pole casts no shadow at noon.
Hawaii is the only US state in the tropics, so it's the only state where flagpoles lose their noon shadows, twice a year.

title: The polar circles
description: The Arctic and Antarctic Circles, at about 66.5°, mark where the Sun stays up or down for a full day at least once a year.

facts.text: The Arctic Circle lies at about 66.5° N and the Antarctic Circle at about 66.5° S.
On a polar circle the Sun stays up for a full day at least once a year and stays down for a full day, too; at the poles this stretches to six months.

title: Time zones
description: Because Earth turns 15° an hour, the world uses 24 standard time zones counted from Greenwich, with borders bent to follow countries.

facts.text: Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, which is 15° of longitude every hour.
Before standard time, communities kept their own local time by the Sun, and the spread of railways made that confusion urgent.
Standard time divides the world into 24 time zones, based on meridians 15° apart counted from Greenwich, each one hour apart.
The 1884 conference that chose the Greenwich prime meridian also adopted the system of standard time zones.
Real time-zone borders bend away from straight meridians to follow political borders.

title: The International Date Line
description: The date line roughly follows the 180° meridian; crossing it westward moves the calendar a day ahead.

facts.text: The International Date Line roughly follows the 180° meridian, halfway around the world from the prime meridian.
Travelers crossing the date line westward move their calendars a day ahead; going eastward, a day back.
The date line bends around land, such as the islands of Kiribati, so each country stays on one date.

title: Cardinal directions
description: North, east, south and west; Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east.

facts.text: The four cardinal directions are north, east, south and west; east and west are at right angles to north and south.
Earth spins toward the east, so the Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west.

title: How a compass works
description: A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field.

facts.text: A compass needle is a small magnet; Earth acts like a giant magnet, and the needle lines up with its magnetic field.

title: Magnetic north vs true north
description: The North Magnetic Pole is not the Geographic North Pole and drifts; the angle between them is magnetic declination.

facts.text: The North Magnetic Pole is not at the Geographic North Pole (90° N), so a compass doesn't point exactly to true north.
The North Magnetic Pole drifts over time.
The angle between where a compass points and true north is called magnetic declination; it varies from place to place, and navigators correct for it.

title: Elevation and contour lines
description: Heights are measured above sea level, and contour lines join points of equal elevation; close lines mean steep ground.

facts.text: Map heights are usually measured above mean sea level.
Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain, stands about 8,849 m above sea level.
On a topographic map, contour lines connect points of equal elevation.
The closer together contour lines are, the steeper the slope; widely spaced lines mean gentle ground.

title: Plateaus, valleys and deltas
description: Three common landforms: raised flat plateaus, valleys carved by rivers and glaciers, and deltas built at river mouths.

facts.text: A plateau is a flat, elevated landform that rises sharply above the surrounding area on at least one side.
Valleys are low areas carved by water and ice: rivers cut V-shaped valleys, and glaciers grind them into U shapes.
A delta is a flat, low plain built at a river's mouth from sediment the slowing river drops.
Deltas are named after the triangle-shaped Greek letter delta (Δ).

title: Continents by size
description: Asia is the largest continent and Australia the smallest.

facts.text: From largest to smallest, the continents are Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
Asia holds almost a third of the world's land.
Australia is the smallest continent, and also the flattest.

title: Oceans by size
description: The Pacific is the largest ocean, bigger than all land combined; the Arctic is the smallest.

facts.text: From largest to smallest, the oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean; its area is bigger than all the land on Earth combined.
The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface.

title: The GPS constellation
description: At least 24 GPS satellites with precise clocks broadcast one-way signals of their position and time.

facts.text: The US keeps at least 24 GPS satellites working, arranged so at least four are in view from almost anywhere on Earth.
Each GPS satellite circles Earth twice a day, about 20,200 km up.
GPS satellites send one-way signals giving their position and the time; receivers only listen and never transmit to them.
The civilian GPS service is free for anyone to use, worldwide.
GPS satellites carry very precise atomic clocks.

title: How GPS finds you
description: A receiver turns signal travel times into distances and needs four satellites: three for position, one to fix its clock.

facts.text: A receiver finds its distance to each satellite from how long the signal took to arrive, since the signal travels at the speed of light.
A precise GPS fix needs four satellites: three to find the position and one to correct the error in the receiver's clock.
A GPS receiver calculates its position in three dimensions (latitude, longitude and altitude) plus the time.

title: Antipodes
description: A place's antipode is the point directly opposite it through Earth's center: opposite hemisphere, 180° of longitude away, about 12 hours off.

facts.text: A place's antipode is the point exactly opposite it on Earth: a straight line between them passes through Earth's center.
An antipode keeps the same latitude number in the other hemisphere, and its longitude is 180° away.
A place and its antipode are about 12 hours apart: when it's noon at one, it's midnight at the other.
Only about 15% of land has land at its antipode; most land sits opposite ocean.
Dig straight through Earth from almost anywhere in the contiguous US and you'd come out in the Indian Ocean, not China.
Spain and New Zealand are near-opposites: most of New Zealand's North Island is antipodal to Spain.

title: Crust and mantle
description: Earth's thin rocky crust sits on the mantle, a thick layer of solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods.

facts.text: Soviet scientists drilled the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia for about 20 years, reaching 12,262 m, still inside Earth's crust.
The Kola borehole's 12,262 m is less than 0.2% of the roughly 6,371 km from Earth's surface to its center.
It is about 6,371 km from Earth's surface to its center.
Earth's crust is about 5 to 10 km thick under the oceans and up to 70 km thick under some continents.
The mantle is about 2,900 km thick and makes up about 84% of Earth's volume.
Mantle rock is solid, but over long periods it slowly flows, at about the rate fingernails grow.

title: Earth's metal core
description: The core is iron and nickel: a liquid outer core that makes the magnetic field and a solid inner core, revealed by earthquake waves.

facts.text: Earth's core begins about 2,900 km below the surface and is made almost entirely of iron and nickel.
The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, and its swirling motion creates Earth's magnetic field.
The inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun, yet it stays solid because of the immense pressure of the planet above it.
Earthquake S-waves can't travel through liquid; the shadow where they vanish on Earth's far side revealed the liquid outer core.
The outer core is the only entirely liquid layer inside Earth.

title: Tectonic plates
description: Earth's outer shell is broken into rocky plates that carry continents and oceans and move a few centimeters a year.

facts.text: Earth's lithosphere, the crust plus the top of the mantle, is broken into large rocky plates that carry the continents and oceans.
The plates move on a slowly flowing layer of the upper mantle, pushed along by convection, heat circulating in the rock.
Tectonic plates move relative to each other at about 2 to 15 cm a year.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 cm a year; over 100 to 200 million years, the Atlantic grew from a narrow inlet into an ocean.

title: Plate boundaries
description: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent ones and slide past each other at transform boundaries.

facts.text: At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart and new crust forms; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the best-known example.
At convergent boundaries, plates push together and crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another.
At transform boundaries, plates slide sideways past each other; California's San Andreas Fault is one.
The Pacific Plate slides northwest past the North American Plate about 46 mm a year, so LA and San Francisco will one day be neighbors.
The San Andreas Fault's plates slide past each other at about the rate your fingernails grow.

title: Continental drift and Pangaea
description: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in Pangaea; the idea was accepted once plate tectonics explained the motion.

facts.text: In 1912, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea.
The name Pangaea comes from Greek words meaning 'all the Earth'.
Pangaea was surrounded by a single global ocean called Panthalassa.
Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago, and its pieces became today's continents.
Most scientists rejected Wegener's idea because he couldn't explain what force could move whole continents.
In the 1960s, seafloor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the missing mechanism, and moving continents became accepted.

title: Evidence the continents were joined
description: Matching coastlines, matching rock layers and fossils like Mesosaurus show Africa and South America were once joined.

facts.text: The coasts of South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces, and their rock layers match too.
Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile that couldn't have swum the Atlantic, are found only in southern Africa and South America.

title: What causes earthquakes
description: Stuck plate edges build up force until rock suddenly slips along a fault, sending out seismic waves from the hypocenter.

facts.text: An earthquake happens when two blocks of Earth suddenly slip past one another along a fault.
Rough plate edges get stuck while the rest of the plate keeps moving; when the built-up force beats friction, the rock slips.
The hypocenter is where an earthquake starts underground; the epicenter is the point on the surface directly above it.
An earthquake's energy spreads out as seismic waves, like ripples on a pond, and seismographs record them.

title: Earthquake magnitude
description: Each whole step in magnitude means about 32 times more energy; the largest recorded earthquake was magnitude 9.5.

facts.text: Each whole-number step in earthquake magnitude means ten times bigger swings on a seismogram and about 32 times more energy.
A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 5 (32 x 32).
The largest earthquake ever recorded struck southern Chile on May 22, 1960, with a magnitude of 9.5.

title: How volcanoes form
description: Magma rises because it is lighter than solid rock and erupts as lava, mostly near plate boundaries where sinking plates melt.

facts.text: Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises; once it erupts at the surface, it's called lava.
The vast majority of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes happen near plate boundaries.
Where one plate dives beneath another, the sinking rock melts and becomes magma that feeds volcanoes.

title: The Ring of Fire
description: A belt of plate boundaries around the Pacific holds about 75% of Earth's volcanoes and 90% of its earthquakes.

facts.text: The Ring of Fire is a string of plate boundaries around the Pacific Ocean about 40,000 km long.
About 75% of Earth's volcanoes, more than 450, lie along the Ring of Fire, and about 90% of earthquakes happen along it.
The Ring of Fire is a horseshoe-shaped belt of volcanoes and frequent earthquakes, about 40,000 km long, around the Pacific Ocean.
About 75% of Earth's volcanoes lie along the Ring of Fire, and most earthquakes happen along it too.
The Ring of Fire runs through Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia.
Japan has 111 active volcanoes, about 10% of the world's.
Indonesia, made up of some 17,500 islands, has one of the most active volcanic zones in the world, running from Sumatra through Java.
The Philippines, more than 7,000 islands, has about 50 volcanoes, more than 10 of them active.

title: Hotspots
description: Some volcanoes, like Hawaii's, form over a stationary hotspot in the mantle, far from plate boundaries.

facts.text: Hawaii's volcanoes sit mid-plate, more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary, over a stationary hotspot deep in the mantle.
The moving plate carries each Hawaiian island off the hotspot and its volcanoes die out, so the Big Island, still over it, is youngest.

title: How tsunamis form
description: Undersea earthquakes lift or drop the seafloor, shoving the whole water column and launching a tsunami.

facts.text: A tsunami is a series of waves caused mostly by undersea earthquakes or volcanic eruptions.
In an undersea earthquake, the seafloor is suddenly lifted or dropped, pushing the entire column of water above it up or down.
Tsunami is a Japanese word meaning 'harbor wave'; the old name 'tidal wave' is discouraged because tides have little to do with it.
Tsunamis frequently strike the Pacific, where dense ocean plates slide under lighter continental plates.

title: How tsunamis travel
description: Tsunamis race across deep ocean as low waves, then slow and grow tall in shallow water; the sea may pull back first.

facts.text: Over deep ocean water, tsunami waves can travel as fast as jet planes.
In the open ocean, a tsunami is at most a few meters high, spread over tens to hundreds of kilometers.
Near shore, a tsunami slows down in the shallower water and builds up higher and higher.
Often the first part of a tsunami to reach shore is a trough, so the sea pulls back far from the beach: a natural warning sign.
The tsunami from Chile's 1960 earthquake crossed the Pacific in almost 15 hours and killed 61 people in Hilo, Hawaii.

title: Mountains from colliding plates
description: When India hit Eurasia, neither plate could sink, so the crust crumpled upward into the still-rising Himalayas.

facts.text: About 80 million years ago, India lay roughly 6,400 km south of Asia, moving north at about 9 m a century.
The Himalayas began to form 40 to 50 million years ago, when India collided with Eurasia.
India and Eurasia have rock of about the same density, so neither could sink under the other; the crust crumpled and thrust upward.
The Himalayas are still rising today, because India is still pushing into Asia.

title: Everest's sea-floor summit
description: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone from an ancient sea floor, full of marine fossils, lifted by the collision.

facts.text: The rock at Everest's summit is limestone that formed on an ancient sea floor, and it holds fossils of sea creatures.
India's collision with Asia thrust the old sea-floor rock upward to Everest's summit.

title: The three kinds of rock
description: Igneous rock cools from molten rock, sedimentary rock forms from pressed layers, metamorphic rock is changed by heat and pressure.

facts.text: There are three main types of rock: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.
Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and hardens, whether as magma underground or as lava at the surface.
Igneous rock that cools slowly underground grows large crystals, like granite; lava that cools fast makes fine-grained rock, like basalt.
Sedimentary rock forms from pieces of other rock or once-living material; as layers pile up, the lowest are pressed into solid rock.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock often built from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures.
Metamorphic rock is rock changed by heat and pressure without melting.

title: The rock cycle
description: Any type of rock can become any other; limestone becomes marble and granite becomes gneiss under heat and pressure.

facts.text: With enough heat and pressure, limestone turns into marble, and granite turns into gneiss.
In the rock cycle, any type of rock can become any other type.
Weathering breaks rock into pieces and erosion carries them away, supplying the sediment that builds sedimentary rock.

title: Weathering and erosion
description: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion carries it away. Water is the main agent, as the Grand Canyon shows.

facts.text: Weathering breaks down or dissolves rock where it sits; erosion wears material away and carries it somewhere else.
Liquid water is the major agent of erosion on Earth; wind and glacial ice erode too.
The Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago; the canyon is about 1.6 km deep.
In floods, the Colorado River carries large rocks that act like chisels, chipping pieces off its bed.

title: Landforms carved by erosion
description: Waves carve caves, arches and sea stacks; wind shapes rock and dunes; glaciers widen valleys.

facts.text: Waves bore caves into sea cliffs; a cave that breaks through becomes an arch, and more wave action leaves rock columns called sea stacks.
Wind is a powerful agent of erosion: it sculpts rock and piles sand into dunes.

title: Iceland's rift
description: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, and over a hotspot.

facts.text: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is splitting as the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart.
Almost all of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is hidden under the sea; Iceland is where it rises above the water.
At Þingvellir, the land between the separating plates has sunk into a rift valley about 7 km wide.
In Iceland, the plates move apart about 2 cm a year.
Iceland's volcanoes are also fed by a hotspot beneath the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

title: The water cycle
description: Water circulates between ocean, air and land, lifted by the Sun's energy and pulled back by gravity, while the total amount stays about the same.

facts.text: Water keeps circulating between the ocean, the air and the land, and the total amount of water in the cycle stays essentially constant.
Energy from the Sun and the force of gravity drive the water cycle.
Water evaporates into vapor, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation such as rain or snow, and moves back across and under the land.

title: Where water vapor comes from
description: Most water vapor evaporates from oceans and other open water, plants add more by transpiration, and a molecule stays aloft only about 10 days.

facts.text: About 90% of the water vapor in the air evaporated from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers; most of the rest came from plants.
Plants release water vapor through tiny pores in their leaves; this is called transpiration.
Once it evaporates, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air on average.

title: Seas and oceans
description: Seas are smaller parts of the ocean, usually partly enclosed by land; the Sargasso Sea is the one exception, bounded only by currents.

facts.text: Seas are smaller than oceans, usually lie where land and ocean meet, and are typically partly enclosed by land.
The Sargasso Sea, in the Atlantic, is the only sea with no land boundary; ocean currents alone define its edges.

title: How deep the ocean goes
description: The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, and its deepest point, Challenger Deep, is about 11 km down: deeper than Everest is tall.

facts.text: The ocean's average depth is about 3,700 m.
The deepest known point in the ocean, Challenger Deep in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, is about 11 km deep.
Set on the floor of Challenger Deep, Mount Everest would still have its peak about 2 km underwater.

title: Surface currents carry heat
description: Winds drive surface currents, which carry warm water from the Equator toward the poles; the Gulf Stream warms northwestern Europe.

facts.text: In January 1992, a container ship in the North Pacific lost a container holding about 29,000 plastic bath toys.
About ten months later the first toys washed up in Alaska, carried by wind and currents; some later drifted into the Atlantic.
Winds drive the currents at or near the ocean's surface.
Ocean currents carry warm water from the Equator toward the poles and cold water from the poles back toward the tropics.
The Gulf Stream is a warm current that flows north along Florida, then turns northeast across the Atlantic.
The warm Gulf Stream helps bring milder winters to Bergen, Norway, than to New York, which is much farther south.
The Gulf Stream forms the western edge of the Sargasso Sea.

title: The deep-ocean conveyor belt
description: Deep currents are driven by density: cold, salty water sinks, keeping a slow global loop moving that takes about 1,000 years.

facts.text: Deep currents are driven by differences in density: cold, salty water is dense and sinks, while warm water stays near the surface.
A parcel of water can take about 1,000 years to complete one trip around the ocean's global conveyor belt.

title: Waves wear coasts away
description: Wind-made waves carry energy to the coast, carving arches that collapse into sea stacks, which erode away in turn.

facts.text: Most ocean waves are caused by wind, through friction between the wind and the water's surface.
Waves carry energy, not water, across the ocean, and can travel across an entire ocean basin.
Wave erosion can carve a sea arch through rock; when the arch collapses, a sea stack is left standing.
Further erosion wears a sea stack down until it disappears.
The Twelve Apostles off Victoria, Australia, are limestone sea stacks; in July 2005 one, about 50 m tall, collapsed into the sea.

title: Longshore drift
description: Waves usually meet the beach at an angle, setting up a current parallel to shore that carries sand along the coast.

facts.text: Waves usually reach a beach at a slight angle, which sets up a longshore current running parallel to the shore.
Longshore drift carries beach sand along the shore, and it can cause significant beach erosion.

title: The longest rivers
description: The Nile, about 6,650 km, is usually ranked longest, but the Amazon (at least 6,400 km) disputes it because experts disagree on where rivers start and end.

facts.text: The Nile, about 6,650 km long, is usually ranked the world's longest river.
The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa into the Mediterranean Sea.
The Amazon is at least 6,400 km long, and some researchers argue it is longer than the Nile.
River lengths are disputed largely because experts disagree about exactly where a river starts and ends.

title: Watersheds and river flow
description: A watershed is all the land draining to one outlet; the Amazon's is the world's largest, and it carries about a fifth of the water running off Earth's surface.

facts.text: A watershed, or drainage basin, is the area of land that drains all its streams and rainfall to one common outlet.
Everyone standing on land is standing in a watershed.
The Amazon is the largest river system in the world, both in the area of its basin and in the volume of its flow.
The Amazon carries about one-fifth of all the water that runs off Earth's surface.

title: How lakes form
description: Lakes fill inland basins; glaciers dug most of them, and rifts in the crust dug others, like Baikal, the deepest and oldest lake.

facts.text: A lake is a large body of standing or slowly moving water that fills a basin inland.
Glaciers have formed more lake basins than any other process, especially in the Northern Hemisphere.
North America's Great Lakes were shaped by a retreating ice sheet.
Lake Baikal in Siberia lies in a rift where Earth's crust is breaking apart; it is the world's deepest and oldest lake.
Lake Baikal holds about one-fifth of the fresh water on Earth's surface.

title: Why some lakes are salty
description: Rivers carry dissolved salt from rocks; a lake with no outlet loses water only by evaporation, so its salt builds up, as in the Dead Sea.

facts.text: Salt in the ocean comes from rocks on land: rain dissolves minerals, and rivers carry them downstream to the sea.
A lake with no outlet loses water only by evaporation, which leaves its salts behind, so the lake grows saltier over time.
The Dead Sea gets nearly all its water from the Jordan River and has no outlet; water leaves it only by evaporation.
The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean.
The Dead Sea's salty water is so dense that bathers float easily, and apart from bacteria nothing lives in it.

title: How glaciers form and flow
description: Glaciers form where snow survives year after year and is squeezed into ice; they flow slowly downhill under their own weight.

facts.text: A glacier forms where snow lasts year-round and piles up; each new layer buries and compresses the older layers into ice.
As buried snow is compressed, it recrystallizes into grains about the size and shape of sugar grains.
A glacier slowly flows downhill under its own weight; mountain glaciers are like frozen rivers of ice.

title: Earth's two ice sheets
description: Only Greenland and Antarctica have ice sheets today; together they hold over 68% of Earth's fresh water, and melting Antarctica would raise the sea about 58 m.

facts.text: Earth has just two ice sheets today: one covers most of Greenland, and the other spans Antarctica.
Together, the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets hold over 68% of the fresh water on Earth.
If the whole Antarctic Ice Sheet melted, sea level would rise about 58 m.

title: How little water is fresh
description: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is ice or groundwater; lakes and rivers hold a tiny fraction.

facts.text: The ocean holds about 96.5% of all Earth's water.
Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh.
Of Earth's fresh water, over 68% is locked in ice and glaciers, about 30% is underground, and a little over 1.2% is at the surface.
If Earth's water filled a 100-liter tub, about 96.5 liters would be ocean, about 2.5 liters fresh, and about 30 mL fresh surface water.
Rivers are the source of most of the fresh surface water people use.

title: Groundwater and aquifers
description: Groundwater fills pores and cracks in rock and soil, like water in a sponge; usable amounts sit in aquifers reached by wells.

facts.text: Groundwater fills tiny pores and cracks in soil and rock; it moves more like water in a sponge than like an underground river.
Groundwater is found in usable amounts only in certain places underground, called aquifers, and people reach it by digging wells.

title: The Nile's yearly flood
description: Each summer the Nile's flood spread dark, fertile silt over Egypt's fields, giving the land its name, Kemet, until the Aswan High Dam ended it in 1970.

facts.text: Ancient Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'black land', after the dark, fertile silt the Nile's flood left each year.
The Nile flooded every summer, and its silt worked as a natural fertilizer that let Egypt grow crops to feed a dense population.
The Nile flooded its valley every year until the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.

title: River valleys and the first civilizations
description: Many of the earliest civilizations grew up in river valleys, where water and fertile soil made farming and irrigation possible.

facts.text: Many of the earliest civilizations, in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus valley and China's Yellow River valley, grew up in river valleys good for farming.
Mesopotamia comes from a Greek word meaning 'between rivers': it is the land of the Tigris and Euphrates.
Farmers in southern Mesopotamia dug branching networks of canals to bring river water to large stretches of dry land.
The Fertile Crescent, often called the 'cradle of civilization', is named for its rich soils; farming and irrigation developed there near its rivers.

title: Ice-age sea level
description: In the last ice age so much water was frozen on land that sea level fell by about 120 m, uncovering the Beringia land bridge between Asia and North America.

facts.text: During the last ice age, so much water was frozen in glaciers that sea level fell by as much as about 120 m.
At the height of the last ice age, ice sheets covered the northern third of North America and much of northern Europe.
The lower sea uncovered Beringia, dry land where the Bering Strait's seafloor is now, linking Siberia with Alaska.
Plants and animals moved across Beringia, and people followed that overland route in search of game.

title: Weather vs climate
description: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average weather of a place.

facts.text: Weather is the atmosphere's short-term conditions, and it can change from minute to minute, hour to hour and day to day.
Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period of time.
A common saying sums up the difference: climate is what you expect, weather is what you get.
Weather tells you what to wear each day; climate tells you what clothes to keep in your closet.
A warming climate still has blizzards and freezing days; over time they happen less often.

title: Climate normals
description: Climate is usually summarized as 30-year averages; NOAA updates its US normals every 10 years.

facts.text: Climate averages usually cover 30 years; NOAA's current US climate normals cover 1991 to 2020 and are updated every 10 years.

title: Sun angle and heating
description: Sunlight arrives more directly near the Equator and spreads over larger areas toward the poles, so the tropics get the most energy; tilt, not distance, drives the seasons.

facts.text: The word climate comes from the Greek klima, meaning an inclination or slope, such as the slope of the Sun's rays.
Near the Equator sunlight arrives almost straight down on a small area; toward the poles it arrives at a low angle and spreads over a larger area.
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the Northern Hemisphere's winter.
Earth's tilt causes the seasons: it's summer in the Northern Hemisphere in June because the Sun's rays hit it most directly then.
The tropics receive the most solar energy, and the Arctic and Antarctic receive the least.
Earth's atmosphere and oceans constantly carry extra heat from the tropics toward the poles through winds, currents and weather.

title: Air pressure makes wind
description: Air flows from high pressure to low pressure; uneven heating by the Sun creates the pressure differences.

facts.text: Wind is air flowing from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure; the bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind.
The Sun heats Earth unevenly; warm air rises and leaves low pressure below it, while cool air sinks and makes high pressure.
Strong heating near the Equator lifts warm, moist air upward like a hot-air balloon.

title: The Coriolis effect
description: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

facts.text: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern; this is the Coriolis effect.

title: The trade winds
description: Steady easterly winds near the Equator, bent by the Coriolis effect, that once carried sailing ships to the Americas.

facts.text: The trade winds are steady easterly winds near the Equator: they blow from the east toward the west.
The trade winds helped sailing ships from Europe and Africa cross the Atlantic to the Americas.

title: Rain shadows
description: Mountains force moist air up, so the windward side gets rain and the leeward side is left dry: a rain shadow.

facts.text: Air pushed up a mountain expands and cools; cool air holds less moisture, so clouds and rain form on the windward side.
As the air sinks down the far, leeward side, it warms and its clouds clear; that dry area is a rain shadow.
Death Valley, in a rain shadow, is the driest place in North America, averaging less than 5 cm of rain a year.
Hawaii's windward sides, facing the moist trade winds, are lush and green; Waikiki and Wailea sit on sunnier, drier leeward sides.
Trade winds pick up moisture as they blow across the ocean.

title: Monsoons
description: Seasonal wind reversals driven by land heating faster than ocean; South Asia's summer monsoon brings most of India's rain.

facts.text: A monsoon is a seasonal change in the direction of a region's main winds; the word comes from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season.
In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean, so low pressure forms over land and draws in moist air from the sea.
South Asia's summer monsoon blows from the southwest, off the Indian Ocean, from about June to September, bringing heavy rain.
About three-quarters of India's yearly rain falls during the summer monsoon.
In winter the pattern reverses: winds blow from the northeast and bring mostly dry weather.
The Tibetan Plateau lies in the rain shadow of the Himalaya, which gives it a dry climate.
Farms in South Asia depend on monsoon rain; late or weak monsoons hurt harvests, and very heavy ones cause floods.
A monsoon is a major wind system that reverses direction with the seasons; the word comes from the Arabic mawsim, 'season'.
Land heats and cools more than the ocean, so monsoon winds usually blow from sea to land in summer and from land to sea in winter.
India's summer monsoon, from about mid-June to early October, brings moist winds from the Indian Ocean and about three-quarters of the country's yearly rain.
Good monsoon years bring bumper crops in India, while poor rains can cause crop failure, especially where there's no irrigation.

title: How tropical cyclones work
description: Tropical cyclones feed on warm ocean water, spin because of the Coriolis effect, and weaken over land.

facts.text: Tropical cyclones form over ocean water of about 27°C (80°F) or warmer; warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses into clouds.
A tropical cyclone becomes a hurricane or typhoon when its sustained winds reach 119 km/h (74 mph).
Over land, a tropical cyclone is cut off from its warm, moist ocean air and its winds weaken.
The Coriolis effect makes tropical cyclones spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern.
The Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator, so tropical cyclones form some distance away from it.

title: Hurricane, typhoon or cyclone
description: The same storm is called a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone depending on the ocean where it forms.

facts.text: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm, a tropical cyclone; the only difference is where it happens.
It's a hurricane in the North Atlantic and central and eastern North Pacific, a typhoon in the Northwest Pacific, a cyclone in the South Pacific and Indian Ocean.

title: Thunderstorms and lightning
description: Thunderstorms need moisture, unstable air and lift; lightning heats air so fast it expands into thunder.

facts.text: A thunderstorm needs moisture, unstable air (warm, moist air below cold, dry air) and lift, such as a mountain slope or colliding air.
As the air keeps rising, the storm cloud grows taller, with strong updrafts and downdrafts inside.
Lightning is a huge electrical discharge between clouds, or from a cloud to the ground.
Lightning heats its channel of air to as much as 30,000°C, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Thunder is the sound of air heated by lightning expanding violently.
Thunder takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 km, so counting from flash to thunder tells you how far away the lightning is.

title: Tornadoes
description: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air from a thunderstorm to the ground; the US has the most.

facts.text: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air that reaches from a thunderstorm down to the ground.
The strongest tornadoes usually come from supercells, large thunderstorms whose winds are already rotating.
The United States has more tornadoes than any other country, most of them on the central plains east of the Rocky Mountains.

title: The Köppen climate groups
description: Köppen's system, built on vegetation zones, sorts climates into five groups: tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.

facts.text: The most widely used climate classification today was introduced in 1900 by Wladimir Köppen, a German climatologist.
Köppen drew his climate borders to match vegetation zones, since what grows in a place depends on its temperature and rainfall.
Köppen's five main climate groups are tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar.

title: Where climate zones occur
description: Tropical climates sit near the Equator, big hot deserts about 15 to 30 degrees out, continental climates inside big landmasses, polar climates near the poles.

facts.text: Ancient Greek geographers divided Earth into five zones: a torrid zone between the tropics, two temperate zones, and two frigid zones beyond the polar circles.
Tropical climates, closest to the Equator, are hot and humid all year, with heavy rainfall.
Dry climates get very little precipitation, and moisture evaporates quickly from the air.
Many big hot deserts, including the Sahara, lie about 15 to 30 degrees north or south of the Equator.
Temperate climates typically have warm, humid summers with thunderstorms, and mild winters.
Continental climates, with warm summers and very cold winters, lie inside large landmasses, far from the ocean's moderating influence.
Polar climates, near the poles, stay cold even in summer: the warmest month averages below about 10°C.

title: The greenhouse effect
description: Greenhouse gases trap some of the heat Earth gives off; without them Earth would average about -18°C.

facts.text: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapor trap some of Earth's heat near the surface.
Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18°C instead of about 15°C.

title: Earth is warming
description: Burning fossil fuels has raised carbon dioxide by more than 50%, and Earth has warmed about 1°C, mostly because of human activity.

facts.text: Carbon dioxide in the air has risen by more than 50% since industrial times began in the 1700s, mainly from burning coal, oil and gas.
Earth's average surface temperature has risen about 1°C since the late 1800s.
Human activity is the main cause of today's warming.
Today's warming is roughly 10 times faster than the average rate of warming after an ice age.
Global sea level rose about 20 cm in the last century, and it is now rising faster.

title: The Hadley cell
description: A loop of air: rising and raining at the Equator, sinking and drying near 30 degrees, returning as the trade winds.

facts.text: In the Hadley cell, warm air rises near the Equator, cools and drops its moisture as heavy rain, then flows toward the poles high in the sky.
Around 30° north and south, the dry air sinks and warms; sinking air blocks clouds, so little rain falls and deserts form.
Near the ground the air flows back toward the Equator, and this return flow is the trade winds.
George Hadley proposed this loop of air in 1735 to explain the trade winds, and it now carries his name: the Hadley cell.

title: What a biome is
description: A biome is a large area defined by its vegetation, soil, climate and wildlife; the five major types are forest, grassland, desert, tundra and aquatic.

facts.text: A biome is a large area characterized by its vegetation, soil, climate and wildlife.
Biomes are usually named for their dominant type of vegetation, such as grassland or coniferous forest.
The five major types of biomes are aquatic, grassland, forest, desert and tundra.
Aquatic biomes include freshwater and marine biomes; marine biomes, which include the ocean, coral reefs and estuaries, cover close to three-quarters of Earth's surface.

title: Climate shapes biomes
description: Temperature and precipitation decide which biome grows where, so similar climates grow similar-looking biomes, even from unrelated plants.

facts.text: A simple way to organize biomes is by their climate: temperature and precipitation.
Wherever a biome occurs on the planet, it has similar types of vegetation and animal life.
Climates that are hot and wet all year grow tropical rainforest, while very dry climates make desert.
The world's main scrublands grow where the climate has mild, wet winters and long, dry summers: the Mediterranean region, California, Chile, South Africa and southern Australia.
Mediterranean-type scrub evolved convergently: different ancestor plants developed similar features in similar climates, so many lookalike plants are not closely related.
California's scrubland is called chaparral, and South Africa's includes the fynbos.

title: Tropical rainforests
description: Tropical rainforests grow in the tropics, warm and wet all year, and are built in four layers from sunny emergents to the dark forest floor.

facts.text: Tropical rainforests are mainly located in the tropics, between about 23.5° N and 23.5° S.
Tropical rainforests have consistently high temperatures and abundant rainfall, with little seasonal variation.
Most rainforests have four layers: emergent, canopy, understory and forest floor.
The forest floor is the darkest rainforest layer: on average only about 2% of sunlight reaches it, so plants struggle to grow there.

title: Why rainforests teem with life
description: Year-round sunlight and moisture let rainforests hold more than half of the world's species on a small slice of the surface.

facts.text: Rainforests cover only about 2 to 6% of Earth's surface, yet more than half of the world's plant and animal species live in them.
Ample sunlight and moisture are the essential building blocks for the rainforest's huge variety of plants and animals.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest.

title: Deserts are defined by dryness
description: A desert is defined by very little precipitation, not by heat, so icy Antarctica is the largest desert and the Sahara the largest hot one.

facts.text: A desert is a place that gets very little precipitation; some authorities set the upper limit at about 250 mm a year.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth.
Inland Antarctica gets only about 50 mm of precipitation a year, almost all as snow, because its cold air holds very little water vapor.

title: How deserts form
description: Deserts form under belts of dry sinking air around 30° to 35° N and S, and in the rain shadows of mountains.

facts.text: Belts of high pressure around 30° to 35° N and S hold dry, sinking air that brings clear skies and arid climates; the Sahara lies in one.
Air rising over mountains cools and drops rain and snow on the way up; coming down the far side, it warms and its clouds fade, leaving a dry rain shadow.
Death Valley, in California and Nevada, is so dry because it lies in the rain shadow of the Sierra Nevada.

title: Grasslands
description: Grasslands grow between forest and desert on the rainfall scale; fire, drought and grazing keep them open, and grass regrows from its base.

facts.text: Grasslands grow where there isn't enough regular rain for a forest, but not so little that a desert forms.
Grasslands exist on every continent except Antarctica, including the prairie of North America, the steppe of Asia and Eastern Europe, and the pampas of South America.
Droughts, fires and heavy grazing favor grassland, while wet seasons without such disturbances favor woody plants.
A grass leaf grows from its base, at or below ground level, and grass can regrow from energy stored in its roots after fire or grazing.

title: Savannas
description: A savanna is a hot, seasonally dry grassland with scattered trees; the largest are in Africa, and fire keeps the trees in check.

facts.text: A savanna is a grassland with scattered trees that grows in hot, seasonally dry climates.
Savannas are warm to hot all year, with rain in only a few months; the dry season is usually longer than the wet season.
The largest areas of savanna are in Africa, whose savannas are home to the African elephant, the largest land animal.
Wildfires in savannas help stop woody plants from spreading, keeping the balance between grasses and trees.

title: Deciduous forests and autumn
description: Winter makes water scarce, so deciduous trees shed their leaves; autumn yellows appear when chlorophyll breaks down and reveals hidden pigments.

facts.text: In winter, freezing leaves water in short supply, so plants without ways to conserve it would lose water.
Before winter, a special layer of cells grows where a leaf's stem joins the tree and cuts the leaf loose.
In fall, as days shorten and cool, leaves stop making food and their green chlorophyll breaks down, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were there all along.
Autumn reds and purples come from anthocyanin pigments that form in the fall.

title: The taiga (boreal forest)
description: The taiga is the largest land biome: a belt of water-saving, snow-shedding conifers across the far north.

facts.text: Conifer needles lose little water: they have a small surface for their volume, sunken pores and a thick, waxy coating.
Snow slides off the peaks of cone-shaped conifers.
The taiga, or boreal forest, is the largest land biome on Earth.

The taiga is a belt of cone-bearing evergreens such as pine, spruce, larch and fir circling the far north, across Canada, Alaska and Russia, with tundra to the north and temperate forest to the south.
Taiga winters are long and very cold, and a lasting snowpack is the norm.

title: The tundra
description: The tundra is cold, treeless land of low plants, found beyond the Arctic Circle and high on mountains.

facts.text: The word tundra comes from a Finnish word for a barren or treeless hill.
Tundra plants grow low to the ground: small shrubs, grasses, mosses, sedges and lichens.
Arctic tundra lies on land above the Arctic Circle; alpine tundra lies high on mountains, where nights fall below freezing.
On the Arctic tundra, only six to ten weeks a year are warm enough for plants to grow.
Trees can't grow on the tundra: the season is too short to grow wood, strong winds dry and batter plants, and permafrost keeps roots from reaching deep enough for support.

title: Permafrost
description: Permafrost is ground frozen for at least two years; only a thin top layer thaws in summer, so meltwater is trapped and the tundra turns soggy.

facts.text: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen for at least two years.
In summer, only a thin surface layer above the permafrost thaws.
Permafrost acts as a waterproof layer under thin tundra soil, trapping moisture near the surface, so the tundra has many wet spots despite little precipitation.

title: Air cools as you climb
description: Near the surface, air cools by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m you climb, so a tall mountain stacks climates on top of each other.

facts.text: Near Earth's surface, air cools as you climb: on average about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m gained.

title: Climbing through climate zones
description: Plant zones stack up a mountain like a trip toward the poles, as Humboldt showed on Chimborazo; trees stop at the timberline, and the zones are moving uphill.

facts.text: In 1802 Alexander von Humboldt climbed Chimborazo in Ecuador; he stopped short of the summit, but his climb stood as a mountaineering record for nearly 30 years.
Chimborazo, in Ecuador, lies about one degree south of the Equator.
On Chimborazo, Humboldt saw plant zones change from tropical plants in the valleys to lichens near the snow line, like a journey from the Equator toward the poles.
In 1807 Humboldt published a cross-section drawing of Chimborazo showing plants at the heights where they grow.
The timberline is the upper limit of tree growth on mountains or at high latitudes, as in the Arctic; where it lies depends largely on temperature.
Humboldt found seed plants up to about 4,600 m on Chimborazo in 1802; in 2012 researchers found them up to 5,185 m, more than 500 m higher, mainly because of warming.

title: Corals are animals
description: Corals are animals: tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and live in partnership with food-making algae.

facts.text: Corals are animals, not plants, because they can't make their own food; they attach permanently to the seafloor, as most plants do.
Corals are made of soft-bodied polyps, most no thicker than a nickel, that build hard limestone skeletons; reefs are the largest structures made by living things.
Algae called zooxanthellae live inside coral tissue and make food by photosynthesis; they are the coral's main food source and give it color.

title: Reefs: crowded cities of the sea
description: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but hold nearly a quarter of its species, in clear, warm, sunlit tropical water.

facts.text: Coral reefs occupy less than 1% of the ocean, yet nearly a quarter of all ocean species live on them.
Reef-building corals grow in clear, warm, moving water in tropical and subtropical seas, where sunlight can reach their algae.

title: Coral bleaching
description: Water that is too warm makes corals expel their algae and turn white; they can recover if the heat eases, or die if it lasts.

facts.text: When water gets too warm, stressed corals expel the algae living in their tissues and turn completely white. This is coral bleaching.
Bleached corals can recover if the stress eases, but if it goes on they eventually die.

title: What a wetland is
description: A wetland is land where water covers or saturates the soil for at least part of the year; marshes are grassy, swamps are woody.

facts.text: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil, or sits at or near the surface, all year or for part of the year.
Marshes are dominated by grasses and other non-woody plants; swamps are dominated by woody plants, shrubs or trees.

title: Wetlands store and clean water
description: Wetlands soak up floodwater like sponges and release it slowly, and filter sediment, pollutants and nutrients like kidneys.

facts.text: Wetlands act as natural sponges, trapping rain, snowmelt, groundwater and floodwater and releasing it slowly.
Wetlands hold water long enough for sediment and other pollutants to settle out, and filter excess nutrients; they've been called the kidneys of our watersheds.

title: Wetlands and wildlife
description: Wetlands are homes and nurseries for a large share of wildlife: over a third of US threatened and endangered species live only there.

facts.text: More than a third of US threatened and endangered species live only in wetlands, and nearly half use them at some point in their lives.
Most commercial and game fish breed in coastal marshes and estuaries, and many US birds, including ducks, geese, hawks, wading birds and songbirds, nest in wetlands.

title: Earth's connected systems
description: Earth works as connected systems of rock, water, air, life and ice (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere) that constantly interact.

facts.text: Scientists describe Earth as connected systems: the geosphere (rock, from the crust to the core), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (gas) and biosphere (life); many add the cryosphere (ice).
Earth's systems all interact with one another; for example, rain falling from the atmosphere links the hydrosphere with the geosphere.

title: Africa, the second-largest continent
description: Africa is the second-largest continent, covering about one-fifth of Earth's land, and flat maps often undersell it.

facts.text: Africa is the second-largest continent, after Asia, covering about one-fifth of Earth's land.

title: Africa across the Equator
description: The Equator nearly halves Africa, the only continent crossed by the Equator and both tropics, so its climate zones are largely mirrored north and south.

facts.text: The Equator cuts Africa almost exactly in half.
Africa is the only continent crossed by the Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
Africa's climate zones are largely mirrored across the Equator: rainforest in the middle, then savanna, then desert, then Mediterranean tips.
The Sahara is the great desert of northern Africa; the Kalahari and the Namib are deserts of southern Africa.
Savanna, grassland with scattered trees, covers almost half of Africa.
Because of western Africa's bulge, more of Africa lies north of the Equator than south of it.

title: The Sahara, largest hot desert
description: A desert is defined by low precipitation; the Sahara is the largest hot desert (Antarctica is the largest overall), and most of it is rock and gravel, not sand.

facts.text: A desert is land that gets no more than about 25 cm of precipitation a year, hot or cold.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth; the Sahara is the largest hot desert.
The Sahara is almost the size of the contiguous United States.
Sand dunes cover only a minority of the Sahara; most of it is rocky plateaus and gravel plains.

title: The green Sahara
description: About 11,000 years ago a wobble in Earth's axis pushed monsoon rains north and the Sahara held lakes, rivers and grasslands before drying out.

facts.text: People once lived, hunted and fished on the shores of lakes in what is now the Sahara.
About 11,000 years ago, the Sahara was green, with lakes, rivers and grasslands.
Rock art from the green Sahara shows elephants, giraffes, rhinos and hippos.
A slow wobble of Earth's axis shifted summer sunlight, strengthening the African monsoon and pushing its rains north into the Sahara.
The rains then retreated, and the Sahara dried out between about 8,000 and 4,500 years ago.

title: The Nile and its branches
description: The Nile flows north to the Mediterranean; the White and Blue Niles meet at Khartoum, and the Blue Nile brings most of the water and silt.

facts.text: The Nile, usually ranked the world's longest river, flows north into the Mediterranean Sea.
The longer White Nile starts at Lake Victoria, the Blue Nile near Lake Tana in Ethiopia, and they meet at Khartoum, Sudan.
The Blue Nile brings the annual flood and provides most of the Nile's water and silt.

title: The Nile flood and Egyptian farming
description: The Nile's annual flood left fertile silt that made farming possible in a desert, until the Aswan High Dam ended the flood in 1970.

facts.text: About 95% of Egyptians live within a few miles of the Nile.
The Nile's annual flood spread fertile silt over the land, which made farming possible along the river.
Ancient Egyptians called the fertile Nile valley Kemet, 'black land', and the desert beyond Deshret, 'red land'.
The Nile Delta's soil is rich because of the river's large silt deposits.
The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, ended the Nile's annual flood in Egypt.
The dam's steady flow lets farmers irrigate all year, but the silt that once fed the fields now builds up behind it.

title: The Great Rift Valley
description: East Africa is being pulled apart as the Somali plate separates from the Nubian plate; the Red Sea is a rift the sea already flooded.

facts.text: In the East African Rift, Africa is splitting: the Somali plate, carrying the Horn of Africa, is pulling away from the Nubian plate.
As the plates move apart, they stretch and thin the crust between them, opening the rift valley.
The Great Rift Valley system stretches from the Middle East in the north to Mozambique in the south.
Volcanoes dot the rift valleys, among them Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya.
The Red Sea formed when Arabia rifted away from Africa and the ocean flooded the valley between them.
If rifting continues, the sea could flood the rift and make the Horn of Africa an island, though not for millions of years.

title: The rift and human origins
description: The Rift Valley yields key early human fossils such as Lucy, and its datable volcanic ash layers let scientists date them.

facts.text: Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton of an early human relative that walked upright, was found in Ethiopia.
Turkana Boy, a 1.5-million-year-old skeleton of an early human, was found in Kenya.
Layers of volcanic ash can be dated, which gives dates to the fossils found between them.
At Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, running water cut through the rock layers and exposed fossils and stone tools.

title: Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak
description: Kilimanjaro, a volcano about 3° south of the Equator, rises 5,895 m and is the highest point in Africa.

facts.text: In 1848 Johannes Rebmann reported a snow-capped mountain near the Equator; the news was not believed for more than a decade.
Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, rises 5,895 m above sea level, the highest point in Africa.
Kilimanjaro stands only about 3° south of the Equator.

title: Africa's shrinking mountain ice
description: Glaciers near the Equator on Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya are retreating; Kilimanjaro has lost more than 85% of its summit ice since 1912.

facts.text: Between 1912 and 2011, Kilimanjaro's summit ice lost more than 85% of its mass.
A drier regional atmosphere brings Kilimanjaro less fresh snow and fewer clouds to shade its ice from the Sun.
Scientists estimate Kilimanjaro's ice could vanish by 2060.
Mount Kenya, Africa's second-highest mountain, sits just south of the Equator and has small, retreating glaciers.

title: The Congo rainforest
description: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest rainforest; bonobos live only south of the Congo River.

facts.text: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest rainforest, after the Amazon.
Bonobos live only in the rainforest along the south bank of the Congo River, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

title: The Congo River
description: The Congo crosses the Equator twice, so part of its basin is always in a rainy season and it flows steadily; only the Amazon carries more water.

facts.text: The Congo River swings through a giant arc and crosses the Equator twice.
The Congo's basin spans both sides of the Equator, so some part is always in its rainy season and the river flows steadily.
The Congo carries more water than any other river except the Amazon.

title: Africa's countries
description: Africa has 54 countries, more than any other continent; Algeria has been the largest since South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011.

facts.text: Africa has 54 recognized countries, more than any other continent.
Algeria is Africa's largest country; Sudan held that title until South Sudan split off in 2011.
The Sahara makes up more than four-fifths of Algeria.

title: Africa's young population
description: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa, the youngest continent (median age about 19); Nigeria has the most people.

facts.text: About 19% of the world's people live in Africa.
Africa has the world's youngest population, with a median age of about 19: half its people are younger.
Nigeria has more people than any other African country.

title: Africa's great cities
description: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities; Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across the Congo River.

facts.text: Cairo, Lagos and Kinshasa are among Africa's largest cities.
Cairo stands on the Nile, at the gateway to the Nile Delta.
Lagos is Nigeria's largest city, but the capital moved from Lagos to Abuja in 1991.
Kinshasa, capital of DR Congo, and Brazzaville, capital of the Republic of the Congo, face each other across the Congo River.
No bridge links Kinshasa and Brazzaville, so boats carry people between the two capitals.

title: The Middle East
description: A loosely defined region centered on Southwest Asia, often including Egypt; much of it is desert, including the Rub' al Khali sand sea.

facts.text: The Middle East has no official border: it is a loosely defined region centered on Southwest Asia, often including Egypt.
Large parts of the Middle East are desert.
The Rub' al Khali, the Empty Quarter of the southern Arabian Peninsula, is the world's largest area of continuous sand.

title: The Tigris, the Euphrates and Mesopotamia
description: Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, is fertile but dry, so farming there relied on irrigation from the rivers.

facts.text: The Tigris and Euphrates rise in the mountains of Turkey and flow southeast toward the Persian Gulf.
Mesopotamia, Greek for 'between rivers', is the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, mostly in modern Iraq.
Southern Mesopotamia has fertile soil but little rain, so farming there depended on irrigation from the rivers.

title: The Dead Sea
description: The Dead Sea lies more than 400 m below sea level, Earth's lowest land, and is so salty that swimmers float.

facts.text: The Dead Sea lies more than 400 m below sea level, and its shores are the lowest land on Earth.
The Dead Sea's level keeps dropping as the water that once fed it is diverted.
The Jordan River flows into the Dead Sea, nothing flows out, and its water is so salty and dense that swimmers float easily.
The Dead Sea sits in a down-dropped block of crust along a major plate boundary.

title: Persian Gulf oil
description: The Persian Gulf countries hold about half the world's proved crude oil reserves, formed from ancient marine life.

facts.text: The seven Persian Gulf countries hold about half of the world's proved crude oil reserves.
Crude oil formed from tiny ancient sea plants and animals, buried under sand, silt and rock and cooked by heat and pressure.

title: Water scarcity and desalination
description: The Middle East and North Africa have very little fresh water, so Gulf countries desalinate seawater using their oil and gas.

facts.text: Kuwait has no rivers or lakes.
Kuwait gets about 90% of its drinking water by desalination, removing the salt from seawater.
The Middle East and North Africa have about 6% of the world's people but less than 2% of its renewable fresh water.
About 96.5% of Earth's water is in the oceans, and ocean water is too salty to drink.
Desalination uses a lot of energy, and the Gulf countries power it with oil and natural gas.

title: The Suez Canal
description: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and Red Seas without locks, separates Africa from Asia and lets ships skip sailing around Africa.

facts.text: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.
The Suez Canal has no locks: the Mediterranean and the Red Sea sit at about the same level.
The canal gives ships between Europe and Asia a shortcut that avoids sailing around Africa's Cape of Good Hope.
The Suez Canal separates Africa from Asia, so Egypt's Sinai Peninsula, east of it, lies in Asia.
The Nile Delta lies just west of the Suez Canal, and the Sinai Peninsula just east.

title: Europe, a peninsula of Eurasia
description: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, bounded by the Urals and three bodies of water, and itself a peninsula of peninsulas.

facts.text: Europe is the western peninsula of Eurasia, the great landmass it shares with Asia.
Europe's eastern border with Asia is usually drawn along Russia's Ural Mountains.
Europe is bordered by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west and the Mediterranean Sea to the south.
A peninsula is a piece of land surrounded by water on three sides.
Europe is sometimes called a peninsula of peninsulas; its major peninsulas include the Scandinavian, Iberian, Italian and Balkan.

title: Europe's four physical regions
description: From north to south Europe falls into the Western Uplands, the North European Plain, the Central Uplands and the Alpine Mountains.

facts.text: From north to south, Europe's four major physical regions are the Western Uplands, the North European Plain, the Central Uplands and the Alpine Mountains.
Europe's Western Uplands are hard, ancient rock shaped by glaciers, which left lakes and fjords.
The North European Plain, low land stretching from the southern United Kingdom east to Russia, is Europe's most densely populated region.
Europe's Central Uplands stretch east to west across central Europe and are heavily wooded.
Europe's Alpine Mountains region includes the Alps, the Pyrenees, the Apennines and the Carpathians.

title: The Alps, Europe's crumpled water tower
description: The Alps are fold mountains pushed up by a fragment of the African plate colliding with Eurasia, and their water feeds rivers flowing to four seas.

facts.text: The Alps arc across Europe from the Mediterranean coast near Nice, France, to Vienna, Austria.
Fold mountains form where tectonic plates are pushed together and rock is folded and crumpled upward.
The Alps are fold mountains, pushed up where the Adriatic microplate, a fragment of the African plate, is colliding with the Eurasian plate.
Mont Blanc is the highest peak in the Alps.
The Alps are the source of the Rhone, the Rhine, the Po and many Danube tributaries, whose waters reach the North, Mediterranean, Adriatic and Black seas.

title: The Rhine and the Danube
description: The Rhine runs from the Alps to the North Sea and the Danube from the Black Forest to the Black Sea; a canal now links them.

facts.text: The Rhine rises in the Swiss Alps and flows north and west to the North Sea, draining through the Netherlands.
The Rhine is one of the world's most important routes for industrial transport.
The Danube rises in Germany's Black Forest and flows to the Black Sea; it is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga.
The Danube passes through 10 countries, and the capitals Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade stand on its banks.
The Main-Danube Canal, completed in 1992, links the Main (a Rhine tributary) to the Danube, so boats can travel between the North Sea and the Black Sea.

title: The Mediterranean, a sea that connected peoples
description: The Mediterranean sits between Europe, Africa and Asia, and ancient seafarers settled all around it.

facts.text: The Mediterranean Sea is bordered by Europe, Africa and Asia.
The Mediterranean meets the Atlantic Ocean through the Strait of Gibraltar, about 13 km wide at its narrowest.
The name Mediterranean comes from Latin words meaning 'in the middle of the land'.
In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates says the people living between the Pillars of Hercules and the river Phasis live around the sea like ants or frogs around a pond.
The Pillars of Hercules are the two headlands at the eastern end of the Strait of Gibraltar.
Ancient Greek seafarers founded colonies across the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts, from Spain and France to Italy and North Africa.
For Greek colonists, trade was usually the first step, and many colonies became trading hubs.
The Phoenicians and the Etruscans also founded colonies around the Mediterranean.

title: The Mediterranean climate
description: Hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters, found around the Mediterranean and at about 30 to 45 degrees latitude on western coasts.

facts.text: A Mediterranean climate has hot, dry summers and cool, wet winters.
Mediterranean climates lie between about 30 and 45 degrees latitude north and south of the Equator, on the western sides of continents.
In summer, a subtropical high-pressure system spreads over Mediterranean regions, bringing sinking air, clear skies and high temperatures.

title: Russia and Siberia
description: Russia is by far the largest country; most Russians live in its European part, while Siberia covers most of the land.

facts.text: Russia is by far the world's largest country, stretching across all of northern Asia and the eastern third of Europe.
Most Russians live in the European part of the country, especially around Moscow.
Siberia stretches from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, and from the Arctic Ocean south to Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China.
In its wider sense, Siberia covers about three-quarters of Russia.
Siberia is sparsely settled, and swampy forest called taiga covers most of it.
Temperatures as low as -68 °C have been recorded in Siberia's Sakha region.

title: Russia's eleven time zones
description: Russia is so wide that it spans 11 time zones, and its longest railway crosses eight of them.

facts.text: Russia spans 11 time zones, from Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea to Kamchatka on the Pacific.
Kaliningrad and Kamchatka are 10 hours apart: when it's 9:00 a.m. in Kaliningrad, it's 7:00 p.m. in Kamchatka.
The Trans-Siberian Railroad runs between Moscow and Vladivostok, the longest single rail system in the world; the trip spans eight time zones and takes about seven days.

title: Asia's regions and empty spaces
description: Asia, the largest continent, divides into East, South, Southeast, Central, West and North Asia, and much of its interior is thinly peopled.

facts.text: Geographers divide Asia into regions including East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, West Asia and North Asia, which is Siberia.
Vast areas of Central and North Asia have remained sparsely populated because of their forbidding climates.

title: Most people on Earth live in Asia
description: About three-fifths of humanity lives in Asia, crowded into South Asia, eastern China and the Pacific coasts and islands.

facts.text: Asia is home to about three-fifths of the world's people.
Asia's people are concentrated in the Indian subcontinent, the eastern half of China, the Pacific borderlands and the islands.
About 90% of the world's rice is grown and eaten in Asia.

title: How the Himalayas rose
description: India collided with Asia 40 to 50 million years ago; the crust crumpled upward, lifting ancient seafloor to Everest's summit, and it is still rising.

facts.text: The rocks near Everest's summit are limestone laid down on the floor of an ancient sea, the Tethys, and they hold fossils of sea creatures.
India drifted north and collided with Asia about 40 to 50 million years ago.
India and Asia have about the same rock density, so neither plate could slide under the other; the crust was thrust upward instead, forming the Himalayas.
The Himalayas are fold mountains, still being compressed as the Indian plate pushes north into the Eurasian plate.
The Himalayas are still rising by more than 1 cm a year.

title: The abode of snow
description: The Himalayas' snow and glaciers feed great rivers, including the Indus, the Brahmaputra and the Ganges.

facts.text: Himalaya comes from Sanskrit words meaning 'abode of snow'.
The Himalayas are drained by 19 major rivers, of which the Indus and the Brahmaputra are the largest.
The Ganges begins in the Himalayas, where its headstream flows out of the Gangotri Glacier.

title: The Yellow River
description: Named for its loess silt, the Yellow River is the cradle of Chinese civilization and 'China's Sorrow', flowing above its plain between levees.

facts.text: The Yellow River, Huang He in Chinese, is named for the fine yellow silt called loess that it carries to the sea.
The Yellow River is often called the cradle of Chinese civilization.
The Yellow River's destructive floods earned it the nickname 'China's Sorrow'.
Sediment has built the Yellow River's bed up above the surrounding land in many places; even at low water it can sit about 5 m above the countryside.
The Yellow River has changed its course across its plain several times, and people have built extensive levees to control it.

title: The Yangtze, the Long River
description: Asia's longest river runs from the Tibetan Plateau to the East China Sea through China's granary.

facts.text: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world, at about 6,300 km.
In Chinese, the Yangtze is called Chang Jiang, the 'Long River'.
The Yangtze rises in the Tanggula Mountains on the Tibetan Plateau and flows to the East China Sea.
The Yangtze basin is China's great granary and home to nearly one-third of the country's people.

title: South Asia's landscapes and people
description: The Indian subcontinent has three great units, the Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Deccan plateau, and India is now the most populous country.

facts.text: India, Bangladesh and most of Pakistan form a subcontinent, set off from the rest of Asia by the Himalayas.
India's landscape has three main units: the Himalayas in the north, the Deccan plateau in the south, and the Indo-Gangetic Plain between them.
The Ganges flows through one of the most fertile and densely populated regions in the world.
In 2023, India overtook China as the world's most populous country, according to the United Nations.

title: Subduction makes volcanoes
description: Where one plate is pushed beneath another, the sinking rock helps make magma that rises and erupts.

facts.text: At a subduction zone one plate is pushed down beneath another, and the sinking rock helps melt rock into magma, which can rise and erupt.
Japan sits where four tectonic plates meet, the Pacific, Philippine Sea, Eurasian and North American, and its volcanoes formed largely along subduction zones.

title: The Alpide belt
description: A second great earthquake belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean and the Himalayas to Indonesia, along the Alpine-Himalayan ranges.

facts.text: The Alpide belt runs from the Atlantic through the Mediterranean region and the Himalayas to Java and Sumatra in Indonesia.
The Alpide belt's mountains are the Alpine-Himalayan ranges, including the Alps and the Himalayas.
The Alpide belt produces about 17% of the world's largest earthquakes.
In Indonesia, the Alpide belt meets the Ring of Fire.

title: North America's reach
description: North America stretches from near the North Pole almost to the Equator, and takes in Canada, the US, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and Greenland.

facts.text: North America reaches to within about 800 km of both the North Pole and the Equator.
North America takes in Canada, the United States, Mexico, the seven countries of Central America and the Caribbean islands, plus Greenland.
Canada is the world's second-largest country by total area, after Russia.
Greenland is the largest island in the world.
Most of North America lies between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer.

title: North America's shape
description: North America has an ancient rock core (the Canadian Shield), old worn mountains in the east, younger taller mountains in the west, and flat plains between.
