facts.text: North America is built around the ancient Canadian Shield, with the old Appalachians to the east, the younger, taller Cordilleras in the west, and flat plains between.
The western mountain belts, the Cordilleras, cover nearly a third of North America's land.

title: The Rocky Mountains
description: The Rockies run some 4,800 km from northern Canada to New Mexico, the best-known range of the western mountains.

facts.text: The Rocky Mountains stretch some 4,800 km, from northern Alberta and British Columbia in Canada south to New Mexico.

title: The Continental Divide
description: A ridge along the crests of the Rockies and the Andes separates rivers that flow to the Pacific from those that flow to the Atlantic side.

facts.text: A continental divide is a ridge that separates a continent's river systems; North America's runs along the Rockies.
West of North America's Continental Divide, water drains toward the Pacific; east of it, toward the Atlantic and Arctic Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico.
The Continental Divide runs from western Alaska along the Rockies, through Mexico and Central America, and down the Andes.

title: The Great Plains
description: East of the Rockies, the Great Plains form a dry, windy grassland that slopes gently down toward the east.

facts.text: The Great Plains lie east of the Rocky Mountains and stretch from the Rio Grande north to the Mackenzie River delta on the Arctic Ocean.
The Great Plains stand about 1,500 to 1,800 m above sea level at the foot of the Rockies and slope down to about 460 m in the east.
The Great Plains get little rain and much wind, and their natural cover is grassland.

title: The Mississippi's watershed
description: The Mississippi and its tributaries drain all or part of 31 states and two Canadian provinces, about 40% of the continental US.

facts.text: The Mississippi drains all or part of 31 US states and 2 Canadian provinces, about 40% of the continental US.
The Mississippi's big tributaries include the Missouri, from the west, and the Ohio, from the east.
The Missouri River begins in the Rocky Mountains of southwestern Montana and is the longest tributary of the Mississippi.

title: The Mississippi River
description: The Mississippi runs from a wadeable stream at Lake Itasca to a vast delta on the Gulf of Mexico.

facts.text: At its source, Lake Itasca in Minnesota, the Mississippi is a shallow, knee-deep river that visitors wade across.
The Mississippi flows about 3,766 km from Lake Itasca in Minnesota south to the Gulf of Mexico.
The Mississippi ends in a vast delta southeast of New Orleans.

title: The Great Lakes
description: Five lakes, Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario, hold about a fifth of the world's surface fresh water and drain east to the Atlantic.

facts.text: The Great Lakes hold about 21% of the world's surface fresh water and 84% of North America's.
The five Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario.
Lake Michigan is the only Great Lake entirely within the United States; the other four are shared with Canada.
Water from the Great Lakes flows east through the St. Lawrence River to the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Lakes dug by ice
description: Massive glaciers scoured and deepened old valleys in the middle of North America, making the basins the Great Lakes now fill.

facts.text: Starting about a million years ago, massive glaciers scoured existing valleys, widening and deepening them into the basins the Great Lakes now fill.

title: How the Grand Canyon was carved
description: The land was lifted into the Colorado Plateau, then the Colorado River cut down through it over the last 5 to 6 million years.

facts.text: The Grand Canyon, in Arizona, is more than a mile (about 1,800 m) deep and about 446 km long.
Between about 70 and 30 million years ago, the region was uplifted into the high, fairly flat Colorado Plateau.
The Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon 5 to 6 million years ago; the sand and rocks it carries do the cutting.

title: The canyon's rock record
description: The Grand Canyon exposes layers of rock with the oldest, nearly 2 billion years old, at the bottom and younger layers above.

facts.text: The oldest rocks at the bottom of the Grand Canyon are nearly 2 billion years old.
In the Grand Canyon's layers, the oldest rock is at the bottom and layers get younger upward; the rim layer is about 270 million years old.

title: Volcanoes of Mexico and Central America
description: Mexico and Central America sit where several plates meet, so volcanoes like Parícutin and Citlaltépetl are common.

facts.text: Parícutin volcano was born on February 20, 1943, in Dionisio Pulido's cornfield in Mexico, and erupted for 9 years, until 1952.
An active volcanic belt crosses central Mexico; its peaks include Citlaltépetl (Orizaba), a volcano and Mexico's highest point.
Some 40 volcanic cones line Central America's Pacific side; the region has frequent earthquakes and eruptions because several tectonic plates meet there.

title: The Mexican Plateau
description: Mexico's heartland is a high plateau between two Sierra Madre ranges, its largest and most densely populated region.

facts.text: The Mexican Plateau, between the Sierra Madre Occidental and Sierra Madre Oriental, is Mexico's largest and most densely populated region.
Near Mexico City, the southern end of the Mexican Plateau rises to about 2,100 to 2,700 m above sea level.

title: The Central American isthmus
description: Central America is a narrow isthmus of seven countries linking North and South America, with a wetter Caribbean coast.

facts.text: Central America is an isthmus that links North and South America; at its narrowest, in Panama, it is only about 50 km wide.
Central America's Caribbean side receives about twice as much rain as its Pacific side.

title: The Caribbean islands
description: The West Indies curve in a long crescent: the big Greater Antilles, led by Cuba, and the smaller Lesser Antilles.

facts.text: The Caribbean islands, or West Indies, form a crescent more than 3,200 km long that separates the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico from the Atlantic.
The Greater Antilles are the big islands of Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico; the smaller Lesser Antilles curve away to the southeast.
Cuba is the largest Caribbean island.
The island of Hispaniola is shared by two countries, Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

title: Hurricane season
description: Hurricanes feed on warm tropical water, so the Atlantic season runs June to November and peaks in September, when the ocean is warmest.

facts.text: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30; it peaks around September 10, with most activity from mid-August to mid-October.
Hurricanes are rotating storms that form over tropical or subtropical waters and are powered by ocean water of at least 26.5°C.
Oceans take several weeks after the Sun's late-June peak to reach their warmest, just as a day is warmest in mid-afternoon, not at noon.

title: South America's countries
description: South America has 12 independent countries plus French Guiana; Brazil covers about half the continent, and Ecuador is named after the Equator.

facts.text: Ecuador sits on the Equator and is named after it: ecuador is Spanish for equator.
South America has 12 independent countries, plus French Guiana, which is part of France.
Brazil covers about half of South America's land and borders every other South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
Brazil's language is Portuguese; Spanish is the main language of most other South American countries.

title: South America's shape
description: South America is broad in the north and tapers south, with the Andes in the west, the Amazon basin in the north, plains in the east and center, and Patagonia in the south.

facts.text: South America is broad in the north and tapers south; the Andes run down its western edge, the Amazon basin fills the north, plains spread through the east and center, and Patagonia lies in the south.
South America is the fourth-largest continent; most of it lies in the tropics, but it reaches south to subantarctic latitudes.

title: The Andes
description: The Andes run along South America's western edge through seven countries, the world's longest continental mountain range.

facts.text: The Andes are the world's longest continental mountain range, running along South America's western edge through seven countries.
Aconcagua, in the Andes on the border of Argentina and Chile, is the highest point in the Western Hemisphere.

title: The Amazon River
description: The Amazon rises in the Andes near the Pacific, flows east to the Atlantic, carries about a fifth of Earth's runoff, and drains the world's largest basin.

facts.text: The Amazon rises high in the Andes of Peru, within about 160 km of the Pacific, and flows east across South America to the Atlantic.
The Amazon carries about one-fifth of all the water that runs off Earth's surface.
The Amazon is the largest river system in the world, both by the volume it carries and by the area of its basin.

title: The Pan-American Highway
description: A road network runs from Alaska to the tip of Argentina, broken only by the Darién Gap between Panama and Colombia.

facts.text: The Pan-American Highway is a road network of nearly 30,600 km, running from Alaska and Canada to the southern tip of Argentina.
The Pan-American Highway's only break is the Darién Gap, about 100 km of roadless rainforest between Panama and Colombia.

title: Australia: a dry continent-country
description: Australia is the smallest continent and one of the largest countries; except for Antarctica it's the driest continent, with a vast arid interior called the Outback.

facts.text: Australia is the smallest continent and one of the largest countries on Earth.
Except for Antarctica, Australia is the driest continent.
Around 70% of Australia is arid or semi-arid.
The Outback is Australia's vast, flat, arid and sparsely populated interior.

title: Australians live on the coast
description: Most Australians live near the coast, especially the fertile east coast, beyond which the Great Dividing Range separates the cities from the Outback.

facts.text: More than 8 in 10 Australians live within 50 km of the coast.
Most Australians live along the east coast, where the coastal rim is relatively fertile.
The Great Dividing Range runs along Australia's Pacific coast, separating the eastern cities from the Outback.

title: Uluru, the rock
description: Uluru rises 348 m from the Outback plain, is only the tip of a much bigger buried slab, and gets its red color from rusting iron.

facts.text: Uluru, in the Outback of Australia's Northern Territory, rises 348 m above the surrounding plain, higher than the Eiffel Tower.
Uluru and Kata Tjuta are the tips of huge rock slabs that continue underground for up to 6 km.
Uluru is made of arkose; its red color is rust from iron in the rock, and grey patches show the rock's original color.

title: Uluru and the Anangu
description: Uluru is sacred to its Aboriginal Traditional Owners, the Anangu; the park was handed back in 1985 and the climb closed in 2019.

facts.text: Uluru has been sacred to Aṉangu for tens of thousands of years, and climbing it was not generally permitted under Tjukurpa, Aṉangu law and culture.
In 1985 the park was handed back to Aṉangu, who own it, lease it to the Australian Government and manage it jointly with Parks Australia.
The climb up Uluru closed permanently on 26 October 2019.

title: The Great Barrier Reef
description: The world's largest coral reef system stretches more than 2,000 km off northeastern Australia, built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps.

facts.text: The Great Barrier Reef, off northeastern Australia in the Pacific's Coral Sea, is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching more than 2,000 km.
The Great Barrier Reef is made up of nearly 3,000 individual reefs.
Corals are made of animals called polyps; hard corals build calcium carbonate skeletons, and colonies of hundreds to hundreds of thousands of polyps cement together to build reefs.

title: Coral bleaching
description: Corals stressed by warm water expel the algae that feed and color them, turning white; prolonged bleaching kills them, and climate change is the reef's greatest threat.

facts.text: Corals host tiny algae in their tissues that are their main food source and give them their color.
When water is too warm, stressed corals expel their algae and turn white; this is coral bleaching.
Bleached corals can recover if the stress eases, but if it continues they die.
The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority names climate change as the greatest threat to the reef.

title: New Zealand's plate boundary
description: New Zealand straddles the Australian and Pacific plates; in the South Island they meet along the Alpine Fault, pushing up the Southern Alps.

facts.text: New Zealand sits across the boundary between the Australian Plate and the Pacific Plate.
In the South Island the plate boundary can be seen on land as the Alpine Fault; off the North Island it lies under the sea.
Along the Alpine Fault the Pacific Plate pushes up the Southern Alps, which rise about 7 mm a year while erosion wears them down at a similar rate.
Aoraki/Mount Cook, New Zealand's highest mountain, is listed at 3,724 m.

title: New Zealand's volcanoes and geysers
description: In the North Island the Pacific Plate slides under the Australian Plate; melting rock feeds volcanoes like Ruapehu and heats water for the geysers and hot springs of Rotorua and Taupo.

facts.text: In the North Island, the Pacific Plate slides under the Australian Plate, and rock melts deep below.
Molten rock under the North Island erupts from volcanoes such as Ruapehu or heats underground water, causing geysers and hot springs around Taupō and Rotorua.

title: High islands and low islands
description: Pacific islands are either high volcanic islands built by eruptions or low coral islands, often atolls ringing a lagoon.

facts.text: High islands, also called volcanic islands, are built up by volcanic eruptions.
Low islands are made of corals; they often form an atoll, a ring of small islands around a lagoon.
Kiribati is made up of 32 atolls and one solitary island.
The Hawaiian Islands are volcanic islands that formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a hot spot, so the islands get older toward the northwest.
The Hawaiian chain stretches from the island of Hawaii in the southeast to Kure Atoll in the northwest.

title: How atolls form
description: A reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks; when the island disappears, a ring of reef around a lagoon remains, as Darwin proposed and drilling confirmed.

facts.text: Charles Darwin proposed that atolls form when a reef fringing a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks, until only a ring of reef around a lagoon remains.
In the 1950s, drilling at Enewetak Atoll went through more than 1 km of coral and reached volcanic rock, confirming Darwin's idea.

title: Polynesian wayfinding
description: Polynesian navigators found their way without instruments by the rising and setting points of stars, ocean swells, homing seabirds and clouds over islands.

facts.text: Polynesia is a triangle of ocean with corners at Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island (Rapa Nui).
Polynesia was settled by long voyages in large sailing canoes that began roughly 3,000 to 4,000 years ago.
Wayfinders using the Hawaiian star compass memorize where stars rise and set on the horizon and use those points to find direction.
When the Sun is too high to steer by, wayfinders steer by the ocean swells.
Seabirds such as terns fly out to sea in the morning to feed and return to land in the late afternoon, so wayfinders can follow them to land.
Swells bent around islands and clouds piled up over them can reveal land that is still out of sight.

title: Hokulea's 1976 voyage
description: In 1976 the canoe Hokulea sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no instruments, showing that Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate voyages.

facts.text: In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, guided by navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia, without instruments.
Hōkūleʻa's 1976 voyage showed that Polynesians could have settled the Pacific by deliberate voyages rather than accidental drift.
More than 17,000 people welcomed Hōkūleʻa when it reached Papeʻete, Tahiti.

title: The Arctic: an ocean ringed by land
description: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, and sea ice floating on it covers the North Pole.

facts.text: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, and its sea ice covers the North Pole.

title: Arctic sea ice
description: Arctic sea ice grows to a maximum in March and shrinks to a minimum in September; the September minimum is shrinking about 12% per decade, and losing reflective ice speeds warming.

facts.text: Sea ice is frozen ocean water; it forms, grows and melts in the ocean.
Arctic sea ice typically reaches its greatest extent in March and its smallest in September.
September Arctic sea ice is shrinking by about 12% per decade, as measured by satellites since 1979.
Sea ice reflects 50 to 70% of incoming sunlight, while the darker ocean reflects only 6% and absorbs the rest, so losing ice lets the ocean soak up more heat.

title: Antarctica's extremes
description: Antarctica is the coldest, driest and windiest continent: it holds the lowest measured temperature, gets so little snow it's a desert, and sends katabatic winds pouring off its ice.

facts.text: Antarctica is the world's highest, driest, windiest, coldest and iciest continent.
The lowest temperature ever measured on Earth, −89.2 °C, was recorded at Vostok station in Antarctica on 21 July 1983.
Air gets colder with altitude, so Antarctica's high elevation helps make it colder.
A desert is defined by low precipitation, usually less than about 250 to 500 mm a year.
Antarctica's snowfall adds up to only about 150 mm of rain a year, making it a cold, dry desert.
Katabatic winds form when air over Antarctica's ice cools, becomes heavier and flows downhill toward the coast.

title: The Antarctic ice sheet
description: Antarctica is a rocky continent under an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick that holds about 90% of the world's ice and makes it the highest continent.

facts.text: Antarctica is a rocky continent capped by an ice sheet up to 4.8 km thick.
The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 90% of the world's ice.
Thanks to its thick ice, Antarctica is the highest continent, averaging about 2,200 m above sea level.

title: Claims on Antarctica
description: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, and the claims of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom overlap.

facts.text: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom.
The claims of Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom overlap on the Antarctic Peninsula.

title: The Antarctic Treaty
description: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty freezes territorial claims and keeps Antarctica for peace and science; the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans mining.

facts.text: The Antarctic Treaty was signed in Washington on 1 December 1959 by twelve countries active in Antarctica, and came into force in 1961.
The Antarctic Treaty holds existing claims in place, and no new or enlarged claim can be made while it is in force.
The Antarctic Treaty says Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only, banning military bases, maneuvers and weapons testing.
The Antarctic Treaty bans nuclear explosions and the disposal of radioactive waste in Antarctica.
The Antarctic Treaty guarantees freedom of scientific investigation in Antarctica.
The Madrid Protocol of 1991 bans mineral resource activity in Antarctica except for scientific research and names it a natural reserve devoted to peace and science.

title: Polar opposites
description: The Arctic is ocean ringed by land and Antarctica land ringed by ocean; the high, ocean-less South Pole is far colder, and the two poles take turns with six months of sunlight.

facts.text: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, while Antarctica is a continent surrounded by ocean.
The South Pole sits on the polar plateau, about 2,800 m above sea level.
In winter, temperatures average about −60 °C at the South Pole and about −40 °C at the North Pole.
The Arctic's ice floats on an ocean that is usually warmer than the air above it, while Antarctica gets little heat from the ocean.
Because Earth's axis is tilted, for six months of the year the Sun never rises over one pole and never sets over the other.

title: How world population grew
description: World population took until about 1800 to reach 1 billion, passed 8 billion in 2022 as lifespans lengthened, and is now growing more slowly.

facts.text: Around 1800, the world population was about 1 billion people.
The world population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022, according to the UN.
Population grew mainly because people live longer, thanks to better public health, nutrition, hygiene and medicine.
Growing from 7 to 8 billion took 12 years; reaching 9 billion should take about 15 years, around 2037.
The UN projects the world population will peak at about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s.

title: Where people live
description: People are spread unevenly: about 60% live in the Asia-Pacific region, India is the most populous country, and about 87% live north of the Equator.

facts.text: The Asia-Pacific region is home to about 60% of the world's population.
India overtook China as the world's most populous country in April 2023, by UN estimates; China's population had peaked in 2022.
About 87% of the world's people live in the Northern Hemisphere, which holds about two-thirds of Earth's land.

title: Why cities grow
description: Cities grow as people move in from the countryside for jobs and opportunities; they began to boom with industrialization in the 18th century.

facts.text: People move to cities drawn by jobs in manufacturing and the professions and by chances for education and entertainment.
Cities began to boom when large-scale industrialization started in the 18th century.

title: Megacities and the largest cities
description: A megacity has 10 million or more people; there were 33 in 2025. By the UN's 2025 count, Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo are the largest, and rankings depend on how a city is measured.

facts.text: A megacity is an urban area with 10 million or more inhabitants.
The number of megacities grew from 8 in 1975 to 33 in 2025, and 19 of the 33 are in Asia.
Tokyo was the world's largest city in earlier UN rankings; the UN's 2025 ranking, made with a new method, put Jakarta first.
The UN's 2025 city figures use one harmonized method for defining cities, fixing inconsistencies in how countries defined urban areas.
By the UN's 2025 count, Jakarta has nearly 42 million people, Dhaka almost 40 million and Tokyo 33 million.
Dhaka is projected to become the world's largest city by 2050.

title: How many countries?
description: The UN has 193 member states and 2 observer states, but lists of countries differ because places like Kosovo and Taiwan are not UN members.

facts.text: The United Nations has 193 member states.
The UN also has two non-member observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine; with the 193 members that makes 195.
South Sudan, independent from Sudan in 2011, is the newest UN member state.
Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008, and Taiwan are not UN members.

title: How borders are drawn
description: Some borders follow natural features like mountains and rivers; others are straight lines such as the 49th parallel; borders drawn without regard to local communities often cause conflict.

facts.text: Some borders follow natural features: the France-Spain border follows the crest of the Pyrenees, and part of the US-Mexico border follows the Rio Grande.
From Lake of the Woods to the Strait of Georgia, the Canada-US border follows the 49th parallel, agreed by Britain and the US in 1818 and 1846.
In the 1800s and 1900s, European countries drew borders in Africa that ignored the Indigenous communities already living there.
Borders drawn without reference to existing communities have repeatedly led to conflict and border disputes.

title: The world's languages
description: Humans speak more than 7,000 languages, at least 40% of them endangered; English and Mandarin Chinese are the only ones with over a billion speakers.

facts.text: More than 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today.
At least 40% of the world's languages are endangered, and each one lost takes cultural and intellectual heritage with it.
English and Mandarin Chinese are the only languages with more than 1 billion speakers each.
English has the most speakers in total, and most of them speak it as a second language; Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers.

title: Language families
description: A language family is a group of languages descended from one ancestor; Indo-European, from Proto-Indo-European, spans most of Europe and much of South and Southwest Asia.

facts.text: Indo-European languages, including English, Spanish, Russian, Hindi and Persian, are spoken in most of Europe and much of South and Southwest Asia.
The Indo-European languages descend from one reconstructed parent language, Proto-Indo-European, probably spoken around 4000 BCE.
The Indo-European family was demonstrated by 19th-century scholars who systematically compared languages' sounds, grammar and vocabulary.
'Three' is drei in German, tres in Latin, treis in Greek and trayas in Sanskrit, all from one Proto-Indo-European root.

title: The major world religions
description: In 2020 Christians were about 29% of the world, Muslims about 26%, the unaffiliated about 24%, Hindus about 15% and Buddhists about 4%; Muslims grew fastest.

facts.text: In 2020 Christians were about 29% of the world's people, Muslims about 26%, the religiously unaffiliated about 24%, Hindus about 15% and Buddhists about 4%.
Christians, about 2.3 billion people in 2020, are the largest religious group.
From 2010 to 2020 Muslims were the fastest-growing major religious group, and the unaffiliated also grew as a share of the world.

title: Where religions are practiced
description: Religions are unevenly spread: most Muslims, nearly all Hindus and nearly all Buddhists live in the Asia-Pacific region, and sub-Saharan Africa now has the most Christians.

facts.text: About 59% of Muslims, 99% of Hindus and 98% of Buddhists live in the Asia-Pacific region.
In 2020 sub-Saharan Africa overtook Europe as the region with the most Christians, home to about 31% of them.

title: The crops that feed the world
description: Just 15 crops give 90% of the world's food energy, and rice, maize and wheat give two-thirds of that; rice, mostly grown in Asia-Pacific, feeds almost half of humanity.

facts.text: Just 15 crop plants provide 90% of the world's food energy, and rice, maize and wheat make up two-thirds of that (about 60% of the total).
Rice feeds almost half of humanity.
More than 90% of the world's rice is grown and eaten in the Asia-Pacific region.

title: How much land feeds us
description: Almost half of the world's habitable land is farmed, and more than three-quarters of that farmland goes to livestock, which supply under a fifth of calories.

facts.text: Almost half of the world's habitable land is used for agriculture.
More than three-quarters of farmland is used for livestock, yet meat, dairy and farmed fish supply less than a fifth of the world's calories.

title: Where resources are found
description: Natural resources are unevenly spread: Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves and the Democratic Republic of the Congo mines most of the world's cobalt.

facts.text: Venezuela has the largest proven crude oil reserves in the world, ahead of Saudi Arabia.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines about three-quarters of the world's cobalt.

title: The resource curse
description: Countries rich in natural resources often grow more slowly than resource-poor ones, partly through conflict over resources; Botswana is a noted exception.

facts.text: Countries with abundant natural resources often grow more slowly than resource-scarce countries, for reasons that include conflict over the resources.
Botswana relies heavily on diamond exports yet is widely seen as avoiding the resource curse by reinvesting mineral revenue in infrastructure, health and education.

title: Scarce fresh water
description: Almost all of Earth's water is salty ocean, and most fresh water is locked in ice, so usable fresh water is a scarce resource.

facts.text: The oceans hold about 96.5% of Earth's water, and over 68% of Earth's fresh water is locked in ice and glaciers.

title: Why people migrate
description: People migrate because of push factors (war, food shortages, floods) and pull factors (jobs, better climate, food supply), within a country or across borders.

facts.text: Push factors, such as war, food shortages or floods, drive people away; pull factors, such as jobs, a nicer climate or a better food supply, draw them in.
Internal migration is moving within a country; international migration is moving to a different country.

title: International migrants
description: About 304 million people, 3.7% of the world or 1 in 27, were international migrants in 2024; the United States hosts the most.

facts.text: In 2024 there were about 304 million international migrants, 3.7% of the world's population, or about 1 in 27 people.
The United States hosts more international migrants than any other country.

title: Forced displacement
description: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people were forcibly displaced; most stayed inside their own countries, and most refugees are hosted by neighbouring countries.

facts.text: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people were forcibly displaced by persecution, conflict, violence or human rights violations.
Of them, 83.4 million were displaced inside their own countries.
A refugee is someone who has fled to a new country; at the end of 2024, 67% of refugees were hosted in neighbouring countries.

title: The shrinking Aral Sea
description: The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake, shrank after its rivers were diverted in the 1960s to irrigate cotton, bringing harsher climate, toxic dust and collapsed fisheries.

facts.text: The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake in the world.
In the 1960s the Soviet Union diverted the region's two major rivers to irrigate desert farms for cotton and other crops.
In 2014 the eastern lobe of the South Aral Sea disappeared completely.
As the lake shrank, local winters grew colder and summers hotter and drier, lakebed dust spread farm chemicals, and the fisheries collapsed.
A dam finished in 2005 helped fisheries in the North Aral Sea rebound.

title: Ocean dead zones
description: Nutrient runoff from farms and cities feeds algae; when they die and decompose they use up oxygen, creating dead zones such as the one off the Mississippi every summer.

facts.text: A dead zone is an area of water with low or no oxygen that can kill fish and other marine life.
Every summer, excess nutrients from farms and cities in the Mississippi River basin feed algae in the Gulf; as the algae die and decompose, they use up oxygen.
